parts.solution_md:
i) The equation for the reaction is:

**H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4 **</sub>**+ 2NaOH → Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>** + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**** [1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the number of moles of NaOH:

moles = concentration x volume in dm<sup>3</sup>

moles NaOH = 0.80 x $\frac{20.85}{1000}$

moles NaOH = **0.01668 (mol)** **[1 mark]**

iii) To calculate the number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>in 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup>:

From the equation, the reacting ratio is 2NaOH: 1 H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

Therefore, moles H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{moles} \mathrm{NaOH}}{2}$

moles H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{0.01668}{2}$

moles H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = **0.00834 mol ****[1 mark]**

iv) To calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid:

concentration = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{dm}^{3}}$

concentration H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{0.00834\times1000}{25.00}$**[1 mark]**

concentration H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>=** ****0.3336 mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports consistently show that the most common mistake in titration calculations is forgetting to use the **mole ratio** from the balanced equation.
> 
> In this case, the ratio is 2:1. You must divide the moles of NaOH by 2 to find the moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> . Always write the balanced equation first and circle the ratio to remind yourself.

- Average titre = $\frac{\mathrm{sum} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{concordant} \mathrm{titres}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{concordant} \mathrm{titres}}$= $\frac{(23.30+23.35)}{2}$ = 23.325 cm<sup>3</sup>;** [1 mark]**
- Moles of NaOH = concentration x volume = $\frac{0.100\times23.325}{1000}$ = 2.3325 x 10<sup>-3</sup> moles; **[1 mark]**
- (The ratio of NaOH : HCl is 1 : 1, therefore) moles of HCl = 2.3325 x 10<sup>-3</sup> moles;** [1 mark]**
- Concentration = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume}}$ = $\frac{2.3325\times10^{-3}}{25}\times1000$ = 0.0933 mol / dm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

  - *Calculating titre volume given initial and final readings*
  - *Identifying results that are concordant / within 0.1 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *

- *Careful**: Do **not **use the rough titre in your average titre calculation *
- *Careful**: For the average titre, divide by the number of concordant results you are using in the calculation **not **the total number of results in the results table*

  - *Calculate the moles of the chemical you know (NaOH, in this case)*
  - *Use the stoichiometric ratio, to deduce the moles of the unknown chemical (HCl, in this case)*

parts.problem_md:
A student performs a titration to determine the concentration of an unknown solution of sodium hydroxide.

The student's method is

- 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of alkali is added to a clean conical flask
- A few drops of indicator are added, and the conical flask is placed on a white tile so that the colour change can be seen more easily
- The burette is filled with acid, and the starting volume is recorded
- The acid is slowly added from the burette to the alkali in the conical flask while the mixture is swirled
- The addition of acid is stopped when the end-point is reached (when the indicator changes colour), and the final volume is recorded
- The steps are repeated until concordant results are obtained

i) Which letter represents the apparatus the student should use to measure exactly 25.0 cm³ of the sodium hydroxide solution?

[1]

![Illustration of four laboratory glassware items: A) Conical flask, B) Beaker, C) Pipette, D) Graduated cylinder; each with measurement markings.](assets/001-illustration-of-four-laboratory-glassware-items-.png)

ii) Which is the best indicator to use?

[1]

A. litmus

B. methyl orange

C. universal indicator

D. iodine solution
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The apparatus the student should use to measure 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> is:
> 
> - **C** / volumetric pipette** [1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The best indicator to use is:
> 
> - **B** / methyl orange** [1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a titration, you need to measure one volume precisely and deliver another volume precisely.
> 
> - A **(volumetric) pipette (C)** is used to accurately measure a fixed volume of one of the solutions to put into the conical flask.
> - A **burette** (not pictured) is used to accurately measure the variable volume of the other solution that is added.
> 
> A measuring cylinder (**D**) or beaker (**B**) are not accurate enough for titration measurements.
> 
> You should be familiar with two titration indicators:
> 
> 1. Methyl orange
> 2. Phenolphthalein
> 
> Litmus is a two-colour indicator, but it is not suitable for a titration as it does not give a sharp endpoint.
> 
> Universal indicator gives a range of colours, but it is not suitable for titrations.
> 
> Iodine solution is an indicator for starch, not for acids and bases.

parts.problem_md:
The student obtains the following results:

| Volume of sodium hydroxide solution used in cm<sup>3</sup> | 25.0 |
|---|---|
| Concentration of sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm<sup>3</sup> | 0.80 |
| Mean volume of sulfuric acid solution used in cm<sup>3</sup> | 13.50 |

i) Write a balanced equation for the reaction between sulfuric acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, and sodium hydroxide, NaOH.

[1]

ii) Calculate the amount, in moles, of sodium hydroxide in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup>.

[1]

iii) Calculate the amount, in moles, of sulfuric acid in 13.50cm<sup>3</sup>.

[1]

iv) Calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction between H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and NaOH is:

**H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>** + 2NaOH → Na**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub>** + 2H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O** **[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the amount of sodium hydroxide in 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup>:

moles= conc x vol in dm<sup>3</sup>

moles of NaOH = 0.80 x 25.0/1000

moles of NaOH = **0.02 mol** **[1 mark]**

iii) To calculate the amount of sulfuric acid in 13.50 cm<sup>3</sup>:

From the equation, the reacting ratio = H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>: 2NaOH

moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{\mathrm{moles} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{NaOH}}{2}$

moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{0.02}{2}$

moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = **0.01 mol** **[1 mark]**

iv) To calculate the concentration of the sulfuric acid in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>:

concentration = $\frac{\mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{vol} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{dm}^{3}}$

concentration of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = $\frac{0.01}{0.0135}$

concentration of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> = **0.74 mol/dm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow error carried forward throughout all steps.
> 
> For example, if you didn't get the equation correct in part i), you can still pick up all the other marks as long as you used your ratio correctly.

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a standard titration calculation. Examiner reports consistently show that the most common mistake is forgetting to use the **mole ratio** from the balanced equation.
> 
> In this case, the ratio is 1:2. This means you need **half** the number of moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> as you have of NaOH.
> 
> A frequent error is to multiply by 2 instead of dividing. Always write down the ratio and double-check which way you need to use it.
